lesson.title: sagen & gestern: the Y→G Twins
lesson.subtitle: say/sagen, yesterday/gestern — and the remaining family words

hook.title: The Y→G Cabinet
hook.content: The last Atlas cabinet holds the y→g twins: English wore the ancient g down to y; German kept it. say ↔ sagen. yesterday ↔ gestern. way ↔ Weg. day ↔ Tag (the double: y→g AND d→t!). rain ↔ Regen. eye ↔ Auge (the g hides mid-word). And the extended family: derive? no — the y-words English still owns: yonder ↔ jener (the far demonstrative from topic 11!). Every English word with a y where a g should be — say, way, day, yesterday, yonder — has its German twin still saying the g.

footnotes.title: Why English Vocalized
footnotes.content: After the Viking and Norman layers, English's palatal g softened to y before front vowels (geaf → yave → gave's old rival, gefeoht? — the clean examples: gear ↔ Jahr's family, yard ↔ Garten!). yard/Garten is the crown pair: the SAME g→y and d→t shifts you know, on a garden word.

pattern.title: The Cabinet Display
pattern.content: Display one: say ↔ sagen — the y→g headliner (ich habe gesagt — you drilled the participle!). Display two: yesterday ↔ gestern — the calendar twin. Display three: way ↔ Weg — der Weg, the path (Ich folge dem Weg — folgen takes dative!). Display four: day ↔ Tag — the double-shift royalty (y→g + d→t). Display five: rain ↔ Regen — y→g with the g mid-word. Display six: yard ↔ Garten (hinted — the d→t + y→g garden pair). Display seven: eye ↔ Auge — the g worn smooth mid-word (die Augen — you own it from the body lessons!). The cabinet closes the Atlas: all nine families, fully displayed.
pattern.linguist_note: The y→g pair is mirror-image to the g→y pair: English day (from dæġ, g vocalized) and German Tag (g kept); but English GET (from *getan) and German bekommen-family? no — get/gotten kept the g! The vocalization only happened before front vowels — which is why 'good' never became 'yood'.

exercises.prompt: The cabinet — match the y→g twins:
exercises.target_answer: sagen / sagte, gestern, der Weg, der Regen, legen / legte
exercises.explanation: English vocalized the g to y; German kept it sounding — the last Atlas cabinet, full. The night exhibits too: der Mond, der Stern, hell (bright), um Mitternacht — and die Nichte, the niece whose n- never shifted at all.

exercises.prompt: The double-shift royalty: 'day ↔ Tag' runs which laws?
exercises.meaning: day ↔ Tag: two laws, one word
exercises.explanation: The d hardened to t AND the ancient g still sounds at the end — day is the double-shift king of the y-cabinet.

exercises.prompt: 'Ich folge dem Weg.' — what grammar does folgen demand?
options: The dative — folgen takes TO someone/something
exercises.target_answer: The dative — folgen takes TO someone/something
exercises.explanation: Following goes TO the followed — the dative receiver law, with folgen joining helfen and danken's club.

exercises.prompt: Which far-distance word (topic 11!) is the y→g twin of 'yonder'?
exercises.explanation: The far demonstrative: *jēnaz gave yon/yonder and jener — the demonstrative map and the y→g cabinet share an exhibit.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'I said the way yesterday' (a little poem)
exercises.meaning: Ich sagte den Weg gestern = Yesterday I said the way
exercises.explanation: Three y→g words in one line: sagte, Weg, gestern — the cabinet, read aloud as a sentence.

summary.outcome: Read every English y as a German g — sagen, gestern, Weg, Tag, Regen, Auge.
summary.takeaway: y→g closes the Atlas: every English y-word has a g-word twin — day/Tag carrying both y→g and d→t.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: prepositions as physical metaphors — über↔over, unter↔under, durch↔through, and the cases they drag along.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from sagen & gestern: the Y→G Twins (Ich sagte den Weg gestern = Yesterday I said the way):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Ich sagte den Weg gestern" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of sagen & gestern: the Y→G Twins without relying on short-term echo.

tag.etymology_derivation: Double shift: d → t and y → g.

morgen.etymology_derivation: Cognate with English morrow (hence to-morrow) and morn — both descend from the Germanic root for "morning". [wiktionary]

legen.context_phrase: Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch.
legen.context_translation: I lay the book on the table.

hell.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *halliz 'resounding'; English bright/light is not cognate — hell is akin to English hall. [wiktionary]

mond.context_phrase: Der Mond ist heute Nacht hell.
mond.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *mānō — the same ancient moon-word as English moon. [wiktionary]

stern.context_phrase: Ich sehe einen Stern am Himmel.
stern.context_translation: I see a star in the sky.
stern.etymology_derivation: Old High German sterno — cognate with English star. [wiktionary]

mitternacht.etymology_derivation: Mitter + Nacht — inherited from Proto-Germanic *midjanahts, the very same middle-night compound as English midnight. [wiktionary]

nichte.context_translation: My niece is playing in the garden.
nichte.etymology_derivation: This form replaced obsolete Niftel in the 17th century; English niece is a Latin loan of the same kinship root. [wiktionary]

nachbar.etymology_derivation: nach (near) + bauer (dweller). Silent gh in neighbor preserves German ch.

vorgestern.context_translation: The day before yesterday the weather was better.
vorgestern.etymology_derivation: vor + gestern — literally fore-yesterday, the twin structure of the archaic English adverb ereyesterday; gestern is the y → g twin of yesterday. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
